Order Flow — What It Is and How to Use It

Follows price_physics_basics.md: if price is a moving object, order flow is the force that moves it. Education, not investment advice.

1. What order flow is

Every trade needs a buyer and a seller. What matters is who was in a hurry.

  • Limit order = "I'll buy at ₹99 / sell at ₹101" — waits in the order book. Passive, provides liquidity.
  • Market order = "buy/sell now at any price" — hits the book. Aggressive, takes liquidity. The aggressor moves price.
  • Order book (market depth): queue of bids (buyers below price) and asks (sellers above price).

A market buy of 1,000 eats the 800 at 101.10 and 200 at 101.20 → price ticks up. Order flow = the stream of these aggressive buys and sells.

2. The physics: F = m·a for markets (Kyle's lambda)

ΔP = λ × (aggressive buy volume − aggressive sell volume)

  • Net order flow = force.
  • λ (price impact) = 1 / mass. Liquid stocks (Reliance, HDFC Bank) = heavy, low λ; small caps = light, high λ.
  • Research (Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov 2014, "The Price Impact of Order Book Events"): order-flow imbalance explains a large share of short-term price changes at the same moment — but its power to predict the next move fades within seconds to minutes.

3. Order-flow measures

MeasureWhat it isReading
DeltaAggressive buy volume − aggressive sell volume in a bar+ = buyers pushing, − = sellers pushing
Cumulative delta (CVD)Running sum of delta through the dayRising CVD + rising price = real buying
DivergencePrice makes a new high, CVD doesn'tPush is weakening (like a car running out of fuel)
AbsorptionHuge aggressive selling but price doesn't fallA big passive buyer is soaking it up → likely support
Order-book imbalance(Bid size − ask size) / (bid + ask) at the top levelsTilts very short-term direction; easily faked (spoofing)
Footprint chartBuy vs sell volume at every price inside each candleShows where the fight happened
Volume profileVolume traded at each price over a periodPOC (busiest price) and value area act as magnets / support
VWAPAverage price weighted by volumeWhere the day's money traded on average

4. Slower order flow (works for swing/delivery, India-specific)

DataWhereHow to read it
Delivery %NSE bhavcopy (DELIV_PER), dailyPrice up + high delivery % = real buyers taking shares home; low % = intraday churn
Futures OI + priceNSE F&O dataPrice ↑ OI ↑ = long build-up · Price ↓ OI ↑ = short build-up · Price ↑ OI ↓ = short covering · Price ↓ OI ↓ = long unwinding
Option OI by strikeNSE option chainBig put OI = support, big call OI = resistance (writers defending)
FII / DII flowsNSE dailyBig institutions' net buying — market-level tide
Bulk / block dealsNSE dailyLarge player entries/exits in a stock

5. How to use it

  1. Confirm a breakout: take an ORB/breakout only if delta (or CVD) agrees with the direction and relative volume is high. Price breaks out but delta is flat/negative → likely a fake breakout.
  2. Spot fakes and turns: absorption at a level, or price/CVD divergence → don't chase; tighten stops.
  3. Place entries/stops: buy pullbacks to the volume-profile POC/value-area edge or VWAP, put stops beyond the level where absorption happened.
  4. Swing filter: prefer breakouts/pullbacks where delivery % is above the stock's average and futures show long build-up.

6. Limits — be honest

  • Order flow is strongest over seconds to minutes — that is HFT territory. Retail speed and costs (see the friction section in price_physics_basics.md) make pure order-book scalping a losing game.
  • The order book can be faked (spoofing, iceberg orders). Executed trades (delta) are more reliable than resting orders.
  • Data: true delta needs tick data with bid/ask. TradingView footprint/CVD needs a paid plan; free OHLCV only allows a rough proxy: delta ≈ volume × ((C − L) − (H − C)) / (H − L) (the accumulation/distribution idea). NSE gives 5 depth levels free; some brokers offer 20+.
  • Use it as a filter on a strategy that already has an edge, not as the edge itself.

7. Puzzle: more buying (positive delta) but a red candle

Real example (footprint, one candle): total buy 107.18K, total sell 79.11K, delta +28.07K, yet the candle closed red. Per price level (high → low), sell × buy: 802×11.0K · 10.5K×45.1K · 7.4K×10.1K · 16.9K×20.5K · 8.5K×3.7K · 4.4K×8.4K · 21.6K×4.6K · 4.4K×3.0K · 4.6K×795.

Why it happens:

  1. Delta counts impatience, not winners. Every share has a buyer and a seller; "buy volume" only means the buyer was the aggressor (market order). Aggressive buyers can be met by a wall of passive limit sellers (often big players, icebergs) who refill the ask — the push is absorbed and price doesn't rise. Force against a wall ≠ motion.
  2. A footprint shows price, not time. The buying happened at the top of the candle (45.1K at the second-highest level), the selling dominated the bottom levels (21.6K vs 4.6K, 8.5K vs 3.7K). Buyers were in charge early, sellers took over lower down.
  3. Liquidity can vanish. If passive buyers cancel their bids, a little selling drops price a lot (λ rises — the object got lighter).
  4. Classification noise. Buy/sell tagging is estimated from bid/ask at trade time; some volume is mis-tagged.

How to read it: positive delta + red candle near a high = buyers absorbed and trapped (the 45.1K bought near the high is now losing). Bearish if the next candle breaks the low — trapped buyers' stop-losses add selling. Invalidated if price reclaims the level where the big buying happened. One candle is never enough; use context (trend, VWAP, key levels, cumulative delta).

8. How to know who was impatient (the aggressor)

The exchange's matching engine knows exactly: the incoming order that matched a resting order is the aggressor. Public/retail feeds usually don't send that flag, so platforms infer it:

MethodRuleNotes
Quote ruleTrade at/above the ask (or above mid) = buyer aggressive; at/below the bid (or below mid) = sellerNeeds bid/ask at the moment of the trade
Tick rulePrice up vs previous trade = buy; down = sell; unchanged = same as lastWorks without quotes; noisier
Lee–ReadyQuote rule, and tick rule for trades exactly at midStandard in research
Bulk volume classificationBar's buy share ≈ Φ(ΔP / σ)For bars without tick data
OHLC proxyBuy share ≈ (Close − Low) / (High − Low)Crudest, free-data only

Example: bid ₹100.00 / ask ₹100.05. Print 500 @ ₹100.05 → buyer paid up → impatient buyer. Print 300 @ ₹100.00 → seller accepted the bid → impatient seller.

What to watch on screen:

  • Time & sales (tape): prints at ask (green) vs at bid (red); speed of prints; big prints.
  • Market depth: ask queue being eaten = buyers impatient; queue that keeps refilling = a patient (often iceberg) seller.
  • Sweeps: one order lifting several price levels at once = very impatient (urgent news, stop-losses, a big fund).
  • Patience signs: large resting orders that don't move, orders added below/above price, absorption.

Limits in India: retail broker feeds send snapshot updates (~1 per second), not every trade, so retail footprints/delta are estimates; tick-by-tick feeds are for institutions. Check each platform's docs for which rule it uses.
